description: Create a gripper, ideally using OpenSCAD that will attach to the SO 101 arm. The gripper should be modeled after the Caledonian Crow, which is generally regarded to have the most dexterous gripper. it doesn't need to be exact but it needs to be that general shape

results.identified_issue:
Request: a gripper for the SO-101, in OpenSCAD, shaped like a New Caledonian crow's beak, "doesn't need to be exact but it needs to be that general shape".

APPROACH. The repo already has a measured, parametric OpenSCAD rebuild of the stock SO-101 gripper at cad/openscad/ (params.scad tagged [STEP]/[DERIVED]/[GUESS], loft-by-hulling-wafers in common.scad). plans/hand_1_0.md section 6 already names OpenSCAD as the source of truth for printable parts, and NOTES.md section 5 says the interesting edits are the blade profile lists because "Hand 1.0 keeps this part's wrist_roll horn interface and servo cradle and throws the jaws away". That is exactly this task, so I did not start a new model: I kept every measured interface and replaced only the two blades. New work lives in cad/openscad/crow/ so the bake-off baseline stays pristine.

BIRD MORPHOLOGY -> PARAMETERS. Three NC-crow-specific traits, each mapped to a list in crow_params.scad:
  1. Straight culmen (unusual for a corvid, which are decurved) -> crow_culmen, a straight chord with ~1 mm convex bulge.
  2. Upturned lower mandible -> crow_tomium runs straight at 5.9 deg for 46 mm then swings 28 deg back toward the upper jaw over the last 21 mm; crow_gonys carries a gonydeal angle at z=84.
  3. Deep base, laterally compressed -> 20 mm deep / 29.6 mm wide at the root, 2.2 mm / 3.4 mm at the tip.
Deliberately NOT included: a hooked tip. NC crows are notable for having LESS hook than other crows; adding one would be less accurate, not more.

KEY DESIGN DECISION — one shared tomial curve. Both mandibles are lofted to the same contact curve, so at crow_opening=0 they are coplanar over 43 mm. The stock jaws instead use a stepped staircase that meets only at the fingertip pads. Line contact is the right call for plans/hand_1_0.md section 2 (paper), and it is what a beak actually does. Cost: the contact faces are coincident at exactly 0, so the interference intersection returns an 0.85 mm^3 zero-thickness film there — reported, not treated as failure.

WHY THE COMMISSURE EXISTS. The lower mandible cannot follow the shared curve all the way down: its neck has to clear the fixed jaw's body as it swings. So crow_lower_tomium ramps from the stock neck face (follower x=-5.6 at z=45.4) out to the shared curve at crow_join_z=62. This is both mechanically necessary and anatomically correct (the gape).

WHY THE NOTCH IS A CROSS-V AND NOT AN AXIAL BORE. A rotating jaw pair can only clamp normal to the tomial plane. A bore down the beak axis (+Z) would look more like how a crow presents a stick, but the jaws cannot squeeze along Z, so it would hold nothing. A 90 deg V across Y gives four line contacts. crow_opening_for_rod(d) derives the required gape from the V geometry, scaled from the notch radius out to the tip radius where crow_opening is measured.

THE INTERFERENCE PROOF. NOTES.md section 5: "Still missing: an interference test." Two forms now exist. Closed form, asserted every compile: the moving jaw rotates about a fixed pivot, so each point moves only along its own circle about that pivot; if radius-from-pivot is strictly increasing along the tomial curve, the rotated lower tomium is everywhere at smaller radius than the fixed one and they cannot meet. crow_r_climbs() asserts that for both mandibles, so a bad row in crow_tomium stops the render. Empirical: check_interference.sh intersects the solids at ten openings. NOTE the trap I fell into — OpenSCAD writes NO FILE when the top-level object is empty, so a naive loop reads a stale STL from the previous iteration and reports phantom interference at every angle. The script rm's/mktemp's per iteration and treats "no file" as the pass condition.

WHY THE STOCK FILES ARE ONLY ADDED TO. I first rewrote fixed_jaw()/moving_jaw() in terms of the new fj_body_solid()/fj_blade() helpers. Output is the same solid (volume identical to 4 decimals) but the extra grouping level changes CGAL's tessellation: fixed_jaw went 5966 -> 5964 facets. Since export/*.stl is committed, I reverted to leaving both modules spelled out verbatim and made the helpers purely additive. A comment in each file says so, so a future agent does not "tidy" it back.
Separately: export/*.stl in cad/openscad/ does NOT reproduce byte-for-byte on this machine even from unmodified git sources — same facet count and same volume, different facet ordering. Facet order is stable run-to-run but not across whatever produced the committed files. Do not treat a byte diff there as a regression; compare volume.

THE FORK/BODY OVERLAP IS INHERITED. Intersecting the full assembly shows overlap in z 13.4-38, y +-24 — identical in the stock gripper (NOTES.md section 6 item 5: fj_fork_clearance() is a square step where the real part has a swept arc). crow_interference() clips below crow_root_z so the test means "the mandibles never touch". Fixing the fork clearance is a job on the stock body and was out of scope for a jaw swap.

IF THIS IS WRONG. Most likely failure modes, in order: (a) the proportions read as a wedge rather than a beak to Jake — the fix is three lists (crow_tomium, crow_culmen, crow_gonys), and the upturn is the lever; I already went from ~0.8 mm of tip deflection to 2.65 mm because the first pass did not read as a crow. (b) jaw_pivot_x/jaw_pivot_z are inherited and NOTES.md section 6 flags them as the one inferred number in the stock rebuild — if they are wrong, both jaw sets are wrong together. (c) 2.2 mm tip thickness may be too fragile; crow_tip_min_t is the knob and the assert enforces it. (d) Untested on real paper and never printed.
results.summary: Built the crow-beak gripper in OpenSCAD at cad/openscad/crow/ — it bolts onto the SO-101 with no change to any mount.
results.detailed_description:
New jaws in cad/openscad/crow/, shaped after the New Caledonian crow's bill: straight culmen, upturned lower mandible, deep base that's squashed flat side to side. Both mandibles are built to one shared contact curve, so unlike the stock jaws it closes along a 43 mm line instead of just touching at the tips — which is the part that should matter for paper.

Nothing that touches the arm moved. The wrist_roll horn pocket, the servo cradle, the cable bore, the fork and the jaw pivot are all included straight from the existing params.scad, so the servo, horn and wiring are unchanged. You will need to recalibrate ID 6 — new jaws, new travel.

There's a 90-degree V notch partway up both jaws, which is the crow's actual trick: it chucks a rod on four line contacts rather than skidding on two flat faces. A 6 mm rod is held with the beak essentially shut. The second picture is that.

Run ./build.sh in that folder for the STLs and pictures. It also runs check_interference.sh, which intersects the two jaws at ten openings across the stroke and reports the overlap volume — that was listed as missing in NOTES.md section 5, and it comes back clear.

Two things I could not check: the beak shape is drawn by eye, not scanned off a specimen, and nothing here has touched an actual sheet of paper. Have a look at the open-jaw picture and tell me whether the proportions are what you had in mind before I print anything.
